questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that $f(\theta) = \sin\theta - \sqrt{3}\cos\theta$,

(a) express $f(\theta)$ in the form $r\sin(\theta - \lambda)$, where $r > 0$ and $0 < \lambda < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Hence,

(b) find the maximum and minimum values of $\dfrac{1}{f(\theta) + 3}$. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a)** Expand $r\sin(\theta - \lambda) = r\cos\lambda\,\sin\theta - r\sin\lambda\,\cos\theta$ and equate coefficients of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ with those of $\sin\theta - \sqrt3\cos\theta$:

$$r\cos\lambda = 1, \qquad r\sin\lambda = \sqrt3.$$

Squaring and adding: $r^2 = 1 + 3 = 4$, so $r = 2$ (as $r > 0$). Dividing: $\tan\lambda = \sqrt3$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, which lies in $\left(0, \dfrac\pi2\right)$ ($\cos\lambda = \tfrac12 > 0$ and $\sin\lambda = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2 > 0$ are both positive, as required).

$$\boxed{f(\theta) = 2\sin\left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)}$$

Check at $\theta = \pi/2$: $f = 1 - 0 = 1$ and $2\sin(\pi/6) = 1$. Correct.

**(b)** Since $-1 \leq \sin(\theta - \pi/3) \leq 1$, we have $-2 \leq f(\theta) \leq 2$, so

$$1 \leq f(\theta) + 3 \leq 5, \quad\text{which is always positive, so } \frac{1}{f(\theta)+3} \text{ is defined for all } \theta.$$

$\dfrac{1}{f(\theta)+3}$ is largest when the denominator is smallest and smallest when the denominator is largest:

- **Maximum** $= \dfrac11 = 1$, when $f(\theta) = -2$, that is $\sin(\theta - \pi/3) = -1$, $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi$ (for example $\theta = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$).
- **Minimum** $= \dfrac15$, when $f(\theta) = 2$, that is $\sin(\theta - \pi/3) = 1$, $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2n\pi$.

$$\boxed{\text{maximum} = 1,\qquad \text{minimum} = \tfrac15}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Find the intervals for which the function $h(x) = x^3 - 3x$ is strictly

(a) increasing

(b) decreasing. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate: $h'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)$. The stationary points are at $x = -1$ and $x = 1$.

Sign of $h'(x)$:

| interval | $x < -1$ | $-1 < x < 1$ | $x > 1$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(x-1)$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+1)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $h'(x)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

**(a)** $h$ is strictly increasing where $h'(x) > 0$: $x < -1$ or $x > 1$, that is on $(-\infty,\,-1)$ and $(1,\,\infty)$.

**(b)** $h$ is strictly decreasing where $h'(x) < 0$: $-1 < x < 1$, that is on $(-1,\,1)$.

$$\boxed{\text{increasing: } x < -1 \text{ and } x > 1; \qquad \text{decreasing: } -1 < x < 1}$$

Check with values: $h(-2) = -2$, $h(-1) = 2$ (rising); $h(0) = 0$, $h(1) = -2$ (falling); $h(2) = 2$ (rising again).
